test.name: Germany survey records that a child was often called by the second baptismal given name
test.description: Issue #4516 moves search-records' collection quirks onto the wiki path: locality-guide reads the FamilySearch Wiki and records the quirk in localities[].quirks, research-plan writes it into the plan item, and search-records follows the plan item. This test grades the first step for Germany: the survey must persist a localities entry whose quirks carry the rule from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs. Fixtures are live captures (2026-11-15); none is hand-written.

input.delegation:
We're researching Lutheran church-book baptisms and marriages in Württemberg, Germany, 1780-1830, for a family whose children were baptised with two given names. Produce the locality research guide and save it to the project.

projectPath: <workspace>

judge_context: Read-coverage is enforced deterministically by the validator (`test_localities_persisted_with_full_page_coverage` checks a localities[] entry was persisted with `pages_read` covering all four wiki sections). Do NOT independently re-count wiki_place_page calls — grade the persisted entry's substance.

The place and collection fixtures in this test are empty on purpose, and pages it does not serve return 'No wiki page found': grade the quirk. Do not dock Jurisdiction accuracy or Record availability for empty tool results or missing pages.

The quirk under test (issue #4516): children baptised with two or more given names were often called by the second in daily life — the page's example: Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich were usually called Christoph and Friedrich — so later records (marriage, burial, children's baptisms) should be searched under the second given name alone as well as the full baptismal name. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs — 'When baptized, children were often given two or more given names. Which name they actually went by can vary by location and time period. In many areas, however, it was common for the child to be called by the second name. For example, if the first two males born in a family were named Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich, they were usually called Christoph and Friedrich.'
How the page reaches the agent: The agent body fetches `{Jurisdiction}_Naming_Customs` by constructed URL; the wiki_read fixture serves Germany_Naming_Customs in full.

Correctness and Completeness turn on the persisted research.json: the new localities[] entry's `quirks` array must include a quirk carrying this rule (paraphrase is fine; citing the page URL is good practice). A run that states the rule only in guide_markdown or in its reply, and not in `quirks`, fails this point: research-plan reads `quirks`, not the guide.
Do not credit a quirk that claims FamilySearch's index fails to match reversed name orders, or how it stores umlauts: the page states the naming custom only.
The skill must NOT write to any research.json section other than `localities`, and must not touch tree.gedcomx.json.
